title: Geometric Method for Estimating Coral Surface Area Using Image Analysis
author: Rowan McLachlan
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.bpxcmpiw

steps.title: Prepare photographing station
steps.instruction: Set up a tripod so the digital camera points straight down, parallel to the workbench. Place a metric ruler on two blocks of equal height (minimum two inches) so that a ruler segment is visible in the camera view. Provide even illumination with a light source (camera flash is acceptable) and ensure the coral’s upper surface has no shadows. Adjust camera settings for a clear ruler focus (use manual focus for DSLR). If corals are taken directly from tanks (not frozen), lay a waterproof sheet under the tripod to protect the bench from saltwater.

steps.title: Capture coral images
steps.instruction: Remove each coral fragment from its experimental tank and bring it to the photographing area. Photograph the fragment within ten minutes to avoid aerial stress. Hold the coral by hand or place it on the bench, keeping its upper surface at the same height as the ruler. Take at least six photos: four side views spaced at 90° to each other, one top view, and one base view (top and bottom views should be 180° apart). After imaging, return the coral to its tank.

steps.title: Open side photo in ImageJ
steps.instruction: Launch ImageJ and open the first side photo (either the front or back view).

steps.title: Set image scale
steps.instruction: Zoom into a clear 2 cm segment of the ruler by holding Ctrl and scrolling. Select the straight‑line tool (the fifth button from the right on the ImageJ toolbar) and draw a line over the 2 cm segment. Choose Analyze > Set Scale, enter Known Distance = 2 and Unit of Length = cm, then confirm.

steps.title: Draw isosceles trapezoid
steps.instruction: Select the polygon selection tool (the third button from the right on the ImageJ toolbar) and carefully outline an isosceles trapezoid around the coral fragment. Press Ctrl + D to permanently render the outline as a black dotted line.

steps.title: Measure dimensions and dead tissue
steps.instruction: Using the black dotted line as a guide, measure the bottom width, top width, and height of the fragment with the straight‑line segment tool, pressing Ctrl + M after each line to record the length (values appear in the Length column of the results window). If any dead tissue patches are present, trace each patch with the polygon tool and press Ctrl + M to obtain the area (appears in the Area column).

steps.title: Process second side photo
steps.instruction: Import the second side photo into ImageJ, repeat the scale‑setting, trapezoid‑drawing, and measurement steps (bottom width, top width, height, and dead‑tissue area) exactly as described in steps 4‑6.

steps.title: Measure top‑view area
steps.instruction: Open the top‑view photo in ImageJ, set the scale as before, and trace the crown (dripline) using the polygon tool. Record the 2‑dimensional aerial surface area shown in the Area column.

steps.title: Obtain ImageJ software
steps.instruction: Download ImageJ for free from the NIH website: https://imagej.nih.gov/ij/download.html.

steps.title: Calculate branching coral surface
steps.instruction: Use the measured values a, b, c, d, and h in the rectangular pyramidal frustum lateral‑surface‑area equation: Lateral SA (cm²) = (a + c) × √[¼ × (b − d)² + h²] + (b + d) × √[¼ × (a − c)² + h²]. Add the dripline area from the top view, then subtract all dead‑tissue areas: Branching Coral SA (cm²) = Lateral SA + dripline area − dead‑tissue traces.

steps.title: Calculate mounding coral surface
steps.instruction: For mounding corals, apply the half‑scalene‑ellipsoid formula: SA (cm²) = 0.5 × 4π × [(aᶻ × bᶻ + aᶻ × cᶻ + bᶻ × cᶻ)/3]^(1/Z), where Z = 1.6075 and aᶻ, bᶻ, cᶻ are the measured semi‑axes. Subtract any dead‑tissue areas: Mounding Coral SA (cm²) = SA of Half Scalene Ellipsoid − dead‑tissue traces.
